settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: validateNextPage does compare against m_engine.getBaseURL() for values containing "://" and replaces non-matching ones with the error page (lines 436-445).
Default nextPage for upload() is the engine's own error page (line 464), so absence of the parameter does not by itself create a redirect.
No attacker-controlled value or concrete caller of doGet/doPost with a tainted nextpage was visible in the read spans.
candidates.description: AttachmentServlet redirects the client to a caller-supplied 'nextpage' value. The helper validateNextPage (lines 434-449) only classifies a value as absolute when it contains the literal substring "://"; in that case it requires the value to start with m_engine.getBaseURL(), otherwise it substitutes the error page. Any value that does not contain "://" is returned unchanged and then passed to res.sendRedirect (doGet line 304 via validateNextPage; upload() line 526 via validateNextPage). In doPost, the value returned by upload() is redirected directly at line 418 (res.sendRedirect(nextPage)), and the RedirectException handler redirects to e.getRedirect() at line 426. Because the guard keys on "://", inputs such as protocol-relative URLs (e.g. "//otherhost/path"), values using backslashes, or other scheme forms without the literal "://" would not be caught by this check and could produce a redirect to an externally controlled location. This is reported as a candidate only: the source read does not show how nextpage is generated by callers, and actual reachability/exploitability depends on the caller and on client behavior.
missing_evidence: The code that constructs the 'nextpage' parameter/field (templates, tags, or callers) was not read.
Whether the servlet container or a filter normalizes/rejects protocol-relative or backslash redirect targets is unknown.
AttachmentManager and other related classes could not be read in this session.
preconditions: An attacker can influence the 'nextpage' request parameter or the multipart 'nextpage' form field (or the redirect target carried by a RedirectException).
The supplied value does not contain the literal string "://" (e.g. a protocol-relative or backslash form) so validateNextPage returns it unchanged.
The affected doGet/doPost/upload path is reachable with that value (views/uploads that trigger the redirect).
candidates.title: Weak next-page validation in AttachmentServlet redirect handling (potential open redirect)

counter_evidence: executeUpload calls AttachmentManager.validateFileName(filename) before storing (line 621), which may reject or normalize dangerous names; its body was not read.
Attachment names may be generated internally rather than directly from user input.
candidates.description: In the download path the servlet sets a Content-Disposition header by concatenating att.getFileName() directly into the header value (lines 269-270: "inline; filename=\"" + att.getFileName() + "\";"). No CR/LF stripping or escaping of the filename is performed within this method. If the stored attachment filename can contain characters such as quotes, semicolons, or CR/LF, the header value could be malformed or split (response header injection / content-disposition manipulation). The response is also forced 'inline' (lines 264-270), which combined with a servlet-chosen content type (getMimeType, lines 377-397) can cause the browser to render attacker-supplied attachment content; however, the mime type comes from the servlet container mapping the filename extension, so this is only a rendering concern and not asserted as a vulnerability. This is a candidate: the actual constraints on att.getFileName() (AttachmentManager.validateFileName) were not readable in this session.
missing_evidence: AttachmentManager.validateFileName implementation and the allowed filename character set were not read.
Whether the servlet container rejects CR/LF inside header values was not verified.
How att.getFileName() is populated relative to the raw multipart file name was not traced.
preconditions: An attachment can be created/stored whose file name contains header-affecting characters (quote, CR, LF) or is otherwise not strictly sanitized.
An attacker can cause a download of that attachment (view permission to the parent page).
candidates.title: Attachment filename interpolated into Content-Disposition header without quoting/escaping in doGet

counter_evidence: The same branch still requires a page 'upload' permission via the authorization manager (lines 691-693), and admin users are presumably trusted.
The extension list defaults to empty (lines 130-141), so for most deployments isTypeAllowed returns true anyway.
candidates.description: In upload() the max-size restriction is only applied when the context does not have admin permissions (lines 488-491: if(!context.hasAdminPermissions()) upload.setFileSizeMax(m_maxSize)). In executeUpload the content-length check and the isTypeAllowed extension check are likewise wrapped in if(!context.hasAdminPermissions()) (lines 637-651). For users that have admin permissions, therefore, neither the configured maximum attachment size nor the allowed/forbidden extension patterns (initialized lines 125-141 and evaluated in isTypeAllowed lines 157-176) are enforced. This is an intentional-looking privilege bypass but is a candidate worth noting: it means an admin-level account can store arbitrarily large files and any file type regardless of PROP_ALLOWEDEXTENSIONS/PROP_FORDBIDDENEXTENSIONS. Whether this is an actual vulnerability depends on the deployment's trust model for admin accounts; no exploit or impact is asserted.
missing_evidence: Definition of hasAdminPermissions and what principals satisfy it was not read.
Deployment guidance on whether admin uploads are expected to bypass these limits was not available.
preconditions: The uploading user's context hasAdminPermissions() returns true.
The wiki relies on PROP_ALLOWEDEXTENSIONS / PROP_FORDBIDDENEXTENSIONS / PROP_MAXSIZE to restrict uploads for all users.
candidates.title: Upload size/extension restrictions and extension check skipped for users with admin permissions

counter_evidence: A concrete authorization check is present: checkPermission(context.getWikiSession(), permission) gates the store (lines 691-722), and a denial throws RedirectException (lines 720-722).
validateFileName is applied to the filename before the attachment is built (line 621).
candidates.description: In executeUpload, the permission enforced is computed from the attachment object (PermissionFactory.getPagePermission(att, "upload"), line 691) and the code first looks up an existing attachment by context.getPage().getName() (line 678). If no such attachment exists, a new Attachment is created using parentPage (the value the upload() method derived from the multipart 'page' field, truncated at the first '/', lines 511-514) as the parent (line 682). The permission check therefore applies to the newly named attachment/parent, but the redirect and the 'page' handling come from separately supplied request fields. The source read does not show a check that the caller is authorized for the specific target parent page before constructing the attachment, and there is no visible comparison that the requested parentPage matches an authorizable page. This is a candidate authorization-consistency concern: the effectiveness depends on how getPagePermission derives the page from att and on the parent-page validation performed elsewhere, neither of which was verifiable here.
missing_evidence: PermissionFactory.getPagePermission implementation was not read, so the mapping from att to the checked page is unverified.
How parentPage and context.getPage() can diverge, and whether that divergence is exploitable, was not determined.
WikiContext.ATTACH page-name derivation was not traced.
preconditions: A user can submit a multipart upload with a 'page' field naming a parent page/attachment combination they wish to target.
PermissionFactory.getPagePermission(att,...) derives its page identity from att in a way not visible in the read spans.
candidates.title: Upload permission and existence check may use a different page than the attachment's parent page
